children.text: eva kramahetum abhidhāya rasaviṣayaṃ lakṣaṇasūtramāha vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having thus stated the cause of the sequence, he gives the defining aphorism concerning rasa: “The production of rasa comes from the conjunction of determinants, consequents, and transitory states.”

children.text: atra bhaṭṭalollaṭaprabhṛtayas tāvad evaṃ vyācakhyuḥ vibhāvādibhiḥ saṃyogo'rthāt sthāyinas tato rasaniṣpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, to begin with, Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa and others explained it in this way: the conjunction with determinants and the rest is, in meaning, the conjunction of the stable emotion; from that comes the production of rasa.
In that case, a determinant is the cause in the arising of the mental state whose nature is the stable emotion.
And the consequents intended here are not those produced by rasa.
For those would not deserve to be counted as causes of rasa.
Rather, they belong precisely to the emotions.

children.text: ye'nubhāvāḥ vyabhicāriṇaśca cittavṛttyātmakatvāt yadyapi na sahabhāvinaḥ sthāyinā tathāpi vāsanātmaneha tasya vivakṣitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those consequents and transitory states, because they have the nature of mental states, are not, indeed, simultaneous with the stable emotion; nevertheless here they are intended as belonging to it in the form of latent dispositions.
Even in the example, within manifestation and the like, one thing has the character of a latent disposition, like the stable emotion.
Another has an arisen condition, like a transitory state.
Therefore it is the stable emotion itself, augmented by determinants, consequents, and the rest, that is rasa.
Let the stable emotion, when unaugmented, remain a stable emotion.
And that applies in both cases.

children.text: mukhyayā vṛttyā rāmādau anukārye'nukartaryapi cānusaṃdhānabalād iti ||
children.translated_text: In the primary sense it is in <s>Rāma</s> and the other original persons to be represented, and also in the imitator through the power of recollective awareness.
This indeed is the position of the ancients.
For so <s>Daṇḍin</s> stated in his definition of ornament:
“Love has become erotic rasa,
through connection with an abundance of forms.”

children.text: adhiruhya parāṃ koṭiṃ kopo raudrātmatāṃ gataḥ
children.translated_text: And, “Anger, having mounted to the highest point, has assumed the nature of the furious rasa,”
and so on.
<s>Śrī Śaṅkuka</s> says: “This is not so.”

children.text: vibhāvādyayoge sthāyino liṅgābhāvenāvagatyanupapatter bhāvānāṃ pūrvam abhidheyatāprasaṅgāt sthitadaśāyāṃ lakṣaṇāntaravaiyarthyāt mandataratamamādhyasthyādyānantyāpatteḥ hāsyarase ṣoḍhātvābhāvaprāpteḥ kāmāvasthāsu daśasvasaṃkhyarasabhāvādiprasaṅgāt śokasya prathamaṃ tīvratvaṃ kālāttanumāndyadarśanaṃ krodhotsāharatīnām amarṣasthairyasevāviparyaye hrāsadarśanamiti viparyayasya dṛśyamānatvācca ||
children.translated_text: For, if determinants and the rest were not connected, the stable emotion could not be understood, since there would be no sign; emotions would have to be stated first; in the established state another definition would be useless; there would follow an infinity of very weak, weakest, middling, indifferent, and other degrees; in comic rasa the absence of sixfoldness would result; in the ten stages of love there would follow innumerable rasas and emotions; and the reverse is in fact observed: grief is intense at first and, over time, is seen to become thin and dull, while anger, energy, and love are seen to diminish when indignation, firmness, and service are reversed.

children.text: tasmāddhetubhir vibhāvākhyaiḥ kāryaiścānubhāvātmabhiḥ sahacārirūpaiśca vyabhicāribhiḥ prayatnārjitatayā kṛtrimairapi tathānabhimanyamānair anukartṛsthatvena liṅgabalataḥ pratīyamānaḥ sthāyī bhāvo mukhyarāmādigatasthāyyanukaraṇarūpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the stable emotion, being apprehended by the force of signs as residing in the imitator, though artificially acquired through effort by causes called determinants, effects having the nature of consequents, and transitory states in the form of accompaniments, and yet not regarded as such, is an imitation of the stable emotion belonging chiefly to <s>Rāma</s> and the like.

children.text: anukaraṇarūpatvād eva ca nāmāntareṇa vyapadiṣṭo rasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And precisely because it has the form of imitation, it is designated by another name: rasa.
For determinants are to be attended to through the power of poetry.
Consequents come from training.
The transitory states come from the power of acquiring artificial and one’s own consequents.
But the stable emotion is not to be attended to even through the power of poetry.

children.text: ratiḥ śoka ityādayo hi śabdā ratyādikam abhidheyīkurvanty abhidhānatvena ||
children.translated_text: For words such as “love” and “grief” make love and the like their denoted object by being designations.
They do not make them known as a form of verbal acting.
For speech alone is not verbal acting.
Rather, verbal acting is what is accomplished by speech.
Just as bodily acting is accomplished by the limbs.
Therefore:
“Though it has grown in itself, though unfathomable, though endless, though great,
grief is drunk up by anger, like the ocean by the submarine fire.”
So it is said.

children.text: tathā śokena kṛtaḥ stambhaḥ tathā sthito yo'navasthitākrandaiḥ
children.translated_text: Likewise, “paralysis produced by grief”; and again, “he who remained thus is begged by ministers,
afflicted by unsteady cries and distressed by fear that his heart will burst, to be roused.”
In such passages grief is not to be acted out.
Rather, it is what is denoted.
“The mass of drops from her tear-water, as she writes, falls and shines;
on my body it seems like the arising of sweat from the touch of her palm.”

children.text: ityanena tu vākyena svārthamabhidadhatā udayanagataḥ suratātmā ratiḥ sthāyī bhāvo 'bhinīyate na tūcyate ||
children.translated_text: By this sentence, however, while it denotes its own meaning, love whose nature is sexual union, the stable emotion belonging to <s>Udayana</s>, is acted, not merely stated.
For enactment is a power of making known, different from denotative capacity.

children.text: ata eva sthāyipadaṃ sūtre bhinnavibhaktikamapi noktam ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason the word “stable” is not stated in the aphorism, even with a different case-ending.

children.text: tena ratir anukriyamāṇā śṛṅgāra iti tadātmakatvaṃ tatprabhavatvaṃ ca yuktam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when love is imitated, its identity as erotic rasa and its arising from that love are both appropriate.
Even practical efficacy is seen in false cognition.
“When two people run toward the light of a jewel and of a lamp, thinking each to be a jewel,
although there is no difference in the false cognition, there is a difference with respect to practical efficacy.”
So it is said.

children.text: na cātra nartaka eva sukhīti pratipattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And here there is not the cognition, “the dancer himself is happy.”
Nor is there the cognition, “this very one is <s>Rāma</s>.”
Nor again, “this one is not happy.”
Nor, “perhaps he is <s>Rāma</s>, or perhaps this one is not.”
Nor again, “he is similar to him.”

children.text: kiṃtu samyaṅmithyāsaṃśayasādṛśyapratītibhyo vilakṣaṇā citraturagādinyāyena yaḥ sukhī rāmaḥ asāvayamiti pratītirastīti ||
children.translated_text: Rather, distinct from correct cognition, false cognition, doubt, and perception of similarity, there is, on the analogy of a painted horse and the like, the cognition: “this happy <s>Rāma</s> is this man.”
Accordingly he says:

children.text: pratibhāti na sandeho na tattvaṃ na viparyayaḥ
children.translated_text: “It does not appear as doubt, nor as reality, nor as error;
there is the thought, ‘that one is this one,’ but not also, ‘that very one is this one.’
Because opposed cognitions are intermingled, it is a confused mingling not discriminated;
by what reasoning could a vivid experience be interrogated?”
So it is said.

children.text: tad idam apyantastattvaśūnyaṃ na vimardakṣamam ityupādhyāyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But this too, the teachers say, is empty of inner reality and cannot withstand critical examination.

children.text: tathāhi anukaraṇarūpo rasa iti yaducyate tatkiṃ sāmājikapratītyabhiprāyeṇa uta naṭābhiprāyeṇa kiṃ vā vastuvṛttavivecakavyākhyātṛbuddhisamavalambanena yathāhurvyākhyātāraḥ khalvevaṃ vivecayanti iti ||
children.translated_text: For thus: when it is said that rasa has the form of imitation, is that said with reference to the spectators’ cognition, or with reference to the actor, or on the basis of the understanding of an interpreter who discerns the actual state of affairs, as when commentators say, “commentators indeed analyze it in this way”?
Now, according to the statement of the sage <s>Bharata</s>, the first position is inconsistent.
For one can say that something perceived by some means of knowledge is an imitation of that thing.

children.text: yathā evamasau surāṃ pibati iti surāpānānukaraṇatvena payaḥpānaṃ pratyakṣāvalokitaṃ pratibhāti ||
children.translated_text: For example, when one thinks, "Thus this man drinks liquor," the drinking of milk, directly observed, appears as an imitation of drinking liquor.

children.text: iha ca naṭagataṃ kiṃ tadupalabdhaṃ sadanukaraṇatayā bhātīti cintyam ||
children.translated_text: But here one must consider what, present in the actor and perceived, appears as an imitation of that.

children.text: taccharīraṃ tanniṣṭhaṃ pratiśīrṣakādi romāñcakagadgadikādibhujākṣepavalanaprabhṛti bhrūkṣepakaṭākṣādikaṃ ca na rateścittavṛttirūpatayānukāratvena kasyacitpratibhāti ||
children.translated_text: His body, what belongs to it, such as the head-ornament and the like, horripilation, stammering and so forth, gestures such as throwing out or bending the arms, movements of the eyebrows, sidelong glances, and the like: none of this appears to anyone as an imitation of love, since love has the form of a mental state.
For these are extremely different from it, being inert, grasped by different senses, and located in a different substratum.
And when the principal thing is seen, there is the appearance of imitation of it.
Nor have any people previously perceived the love residing in <s>Rāma</s>.

children.text: etena rāmānukāro naṭa ityapi nirastaḥ pravādaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this the common saying that the actor is an imitation of <s>Rāma</s> is also refuted.

children.text: atha naṭagatā cittavṛttireva pratipannā satī ratyanukāraḥ śṛṅgāra ityucyate tatrāpi kimātmakatvena sā pratīyata iti cintyam ||
children.translated_text: Now if it is said that the very mental state belonging to the actor, when apprehended, is an imitation of love and is called <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic rasa), then here too it must be considered in what nature that state is perceived.

children.text: nanu pramadādibhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ kaṭākṣādibhiḥ kāryaiḥ dhṛtyādibhiśca sahacāribhirliṅgabhūtairyā laukikī kāryarūpā kāraṇarūpā sahacārirūpā ca cittavṛttiḥ pratītiyogyā tadātmakatvena sā naṭacittavṛttiḥ pratibhāti hanta tarhi ratyākāreṇaiva sā pratipanneti dūre ratyanukaraṇatāvācoyuktiḥ
children.translated_text: One may object: the actor's mental state appears as having the nature of an ordinary mental state fit to be cognized, which has the form of an effect, a cause, and an accompanying factor, through causes such as women, through effects such as sidelong glances, and through accompanying signs such as fortitude. Very well then: in that case it has been apprehended precisely in the form of love, and the verbal device of saying that it is an imitation of love is far removed.
One may object: those <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) and the rest are real in the thing imitated.
But here, in the imitator, they are not so; that is the distinction.
Let it be so.

children.text: kiṃtu te hi vibhāvādayo 'tatkāraṇātatkāryātatsahacārarūpā api kāvyaśikṣādibalopakalpitāḥ kṛtrimāḥ santaḥ kiṃ kṛtrimatvena sāmājikaiḥ gṛhyante na vā ||
children.translated_text: But then, although those <s>vibhāvas</s> and the rest do not have the form of its causes, its effects, or its accompaniments, they are artificially produced by the force of poetic training and the like. Are they grasped by the spectators as artificial, or not?

children.text: yadi gṛhyante tadā taiḥ kathaṃ rateravagatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: If they are grasped as artificial, then how can love be understood through them?
One may object: for just this reason, what is being perceived is the cause of the cognition that it is an imitation of love.

children.text: kāraṇāntaraprabhaveṣu hi kāryeṣu suśikṣitena na tathā jñāne vastvantarasyānumānaṃ tāvadyuktam ||
children.translated_text: For in the case of effects produced by another cause, it is not at all reasonable that a well-trained person, knowing them as they really are, should infer some other thing.
But an untrained person may infer that very well-known cause.
For example, from a particular scorpion one infers dung itself.
But an inference of that very scorpion would be a false cognition.

children.text: yatrāpi liṅgajñānaṃ mithyā tatrāpi na tadābhāsānumānam ayuktam ||
children.translated_text: Even where the cognition of the sign is false, an inference based on that semblance is not thereby reasonable.

children.text: na hi bāṣpāddhūmatvena jñātādanukārapratibhāsamānādapi liṅgāttadanukārānumānaṃ yuktam ||
children.translated_text: For from steam, known as smoke, even though it appears as an imitation, it is not reasonable to infer an imitation of that sign.

children.text: dhūmānukāratvena hi jñāyamānān nīhārān nāṭyagnyanukārajapāpuṣpapratītir dṛṣṭā ||
children.translated_text: Indeed, from mist known as an imitation of smoke, one is seen to have the cognition of a hibiscus flower as an imitation of dramatic fire.
One may object: even when not angry, an actor appears as though angry.
True.
He is similar to an angry man.
And the similarity is due to frowning and the like.
Just as a gayal is like a cow because of its face and so on.
By that much there is no imitation at all.
Nor do the spectators have a cognition of similarity.

children.text: sāmājikānāṃ ca na bhāvaśūnyā nartake pratipattirityucyate ||
children.translated_text: And it is said that the spectators do not have an apprehension of an actor devoid of emotion.

children.text: atha ca tadanukārapratibhāsa iti riktā vācoyuktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Yet to say that there is an appearance of imitation of that is an empty verbal device.

children.text: yaccoktaṃ rāmo'yamityasti pratipattiḥ tad api yadi tadātveti niścitaṃ taduttarakālabhāvibādhakavaidhuryābhāve kathaṃ na tattvajñānaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: And as for the statement that there is the apprehension "This is <s>Rāma</s>," if that is determined at that very time, then, in the absence of a subsequent defeater, how would it not be true cognition?
Or, if a defeater exists, how would it not be false cognition?

children.text: vāstavena ca vṛtte bādhakānudaye'pi mithyājñānameva syāt ||
children.translated_text: And with respect to an actual event, even if no defeater arose, it would still be false cognition.
Therefore the claim, "because of a mingling of opposed cognitions," is invalid.
And with another dancer too there is the apprehension "This is <s>Rāma</s>."
From that it follows that <s>Rāma</s>-hood is a general form.

children.text: yaccocyate vibhāvāḥ kāvyād anusaṃdhīyante iti tadapi na vidmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And as for what is said, that the <s>vibhāvas</s> are connected through poetry, that too we do not understand.

children.text: na hi mameyaṃ sītā kācit iti svātmīyatvena pratipattirnaṭasya ||
children.translated_text: For the actor does not apprehend, as belonging to himself, "This is some <s>Sītā</s> of mine."

children.text: atha sāmājikasya tathā pratītiyogyāḥ kriyanta ityetadevānusaṃdhānam ucyate tarhi sthāyini sutarām anusaṃdhānaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: But if making them fit to be perceived in that way by the spectator is what is called such connection, then there would be still stronger connection with the <s>sthāyin</s> (stable emotion).

children.text: tasyaiva hi mukhyatvena asminnayam iti sāmājikānāṃ pratipattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: For it is chiefly with reference to that very thing that the spectators have the apprehension, "this is in this person."

children.text: yattu vāgvācikam ityādinā bhedābhidhānasaṃrambhagarbhamahīyān abhinayarūpatāvivekaḥ kṛtaḥ sa uttaratra svāvasare carcayiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: But the great analysis of the nature of <s>abhinaya</s> (dramatic representation), full of eagerness to state divisions by expressions such as "verbal speech" and so on, will be discussed later in its own proper place.
Therefore, according to the spectators' cognition, it is invalid to say that <s>rasa</s> is the imitation of a <s>sthāyin</s> (stable emotion).
Nor does the actor have such an apprehension:
"I am imitating <s>Rāma</s> or his mental state."

children.text: sadṛśakaraṇaṃ hi tāvadanukaraṇamanupalabdhaprakṛtinā na śakyaṃ kartum ||
children.translated_text: For producing something similar, which is what imitation first of all is, cannot be done by someone who has not perceived the original.
If, however, later production is imitation, then in ordinary life too the character of imitation would be overextended.

children.text: atha na niyatasya kasyacidanukāraḥ api tūttamaprakṛteḥ śokamanukaroti tarhi keneti cintyam ||
children.translated_text: Or if it is not the imitation of any determinate thing, but rather he imitates the grief of a noble character, then one must consider by what he does so.
Not, to begin with, by grief, since he does not possess it.
Nor is there imitation of grief by the falling of tears and the like, because, as has been said, those are quite different from grief.
There would be this much: 'I am imitating those consequents of grief that belong to a person of excellent nature.'
Even there, of which person of excellent nature?

children.text: yasya kasyaciditi cetso'pi viśiṣṭatāṃ vinā kathaṃ buddhāvāropayituṃ śakyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If one says, 'of someone or other,' then how can even he be superimposed on cognition without any particularity?

children.text: ya evaṃ roditīti cetsvātmāpi madhye naṭasyānupraviṣṭa iti galito'nukāryānukartṛbhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If one says, 'of one who weeps in this way,' then the actor's own self too has entered into the middle, and the relation of imitated and imitator has collapsed.

children.text: kiṃca naṭaḥ śikṣāvaśāt svavibhāvasmaraṇāc cittavṛttisādhāraṇībhāvena hṛdayasaṃvādāt kevalam anubhāvān pradarśayan kāvyamupacitakākuprabhṛtyupaskāreṇa paṭhaṃśceṣṭata ityetāvanmātre'sya pratītir natvanukāraṃ vedayate ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, the actor, under the control of training, from recollection of his own determinants, from the universalization of the mental state, and from consonance with the heart, merely displays the consequents; and, reciting the poem with the auxiliaries such as fully developed intonation, he acts. His cognition is only so much; it does not make him aware of an imitation.
For the imitation of <s>Rāma</s>'s action is not like the imitation of the costume of a beloved woman.
And this too has been shown by us in the first chapter.
Nor is its being an imitation based on conformity with the actual course of events.
For what is being experienced cannot properly have the status of an actual event.
And what the actual event is, we shall show.

children.text: na ca munivacanam evaṃvidhamasti kvacitsthāyyanukaraṇaṃ rasā iti ||
children.translated_text: Nor is there anywhere such a statement of the sage as, 'rasas are the imitation of stable emotions.'
Nor is any indication of the sage found in support of this meaning.

On the contrary, the treatment of fixed songs, varieties of rhythm, dependence on the limbs of lāsya, and so on is an indication of the opposite; we shall elaborate this at the end of the chapter on the juncture-limbs.
But statements such as 'the imitation of the seven continents' can also be explained otherwise.
And even if that were imitation, where is there another name in cases such as the imitation of a beloved woman's costume and gait?
As for what is said, that something is 'cow' and so on only when combined with pigments such as orpiment and the like:
If there the intended meaning is 'being manifested,'
that is wrong.

children.text: na hi sindūrādibhiḥ pāramārthiko gaurabhivyajyate pradīpādibhir iva ||
children.translated_text: For a real cow is not manifested by cinnabar and the like, as by lamps and the like.
Rather, a particular aggregate resembling it is produced.

children.text: ata eva hi sindūrādayo gavāvayavasaṃniveśasadṛśena saṃniveśaviśeṣeṇāvasthitā gosadṛgiti pratibhāsasya viṣayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Precisely for this reason, cinnabar and the other pigments, arranged in a particular configuration similar to the arrangement of the limbs of a cow, are the object of the appearance, 'this resembles a cow.'
The aggregate of determinants and so on is not like this, apprehended through the cognition that it resembles love.
Therefore the statement 'rasas are the imitation of emotions' is wrong.
But the one by whom it was said that the externally existing complex of objects, endowed with the power to generate pleasure and pain, is itself external;
and that, from the Sāṃkhya point of view, rasa has the nature of pleasure and pain;
and that in that complex the determinants occupy the place of parts;
while the consequents and transitory states are the conditioners;
and the stable emotions are internal, born from that complex, and have the nature of pleasure and pain:

children.text: tena sthāyibhāvān rasatvam ityādāvupacāramaṅgīkurvatā granthavirodhaṃ svayameva budhyamānena dūṣaṇāviṣkaraṇamaurkhyāt prāmāṇiko janaḥ parirakṣita iti kimasyocyate ||
children.translated_text: Since he accepts metaphorical usage in statements such as 'the stable emotions have the status of rasa,' and himself understands the contradiction with the treatise, authoritative people have been spared the folly of displaying objections. What can be said to him?
But as for what especially entails, for us, such faults as disparity in cognition, what is there to be said here?
<s>Bhaṭṭanāyaka</s>, however, says: rasa is not perceived.
It is not produced.
It is not manifested.

children.text: svagatatvena hi pratītau karuṇe duḥkhitvaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: For if it were cognized as belonging to oneself, then in the pathetic rasa one would be sorrowful.
And that cognition is not reasonable,
because <s>Sītā</s> and the others are not determinants, and because there is no awareness of the recollection of one's own beloved.
Because, in the case of deities and the like, universalization is impossible.
Because such things as crossing the ocean are extraordinary.
Nor is there recollection of <s>Rāma</s>, who possessed that.
Because he has not been directly apprehended.

children.text: na ca śabdānumānādibhyaḥ tatpratītau lokasya sarasatā prayuktā pratyakṣādiva ||
children.translated_text: And if the cognition of him arises from words, inference, and the like, the relish of people is not brought about as it is from direct perception and the like.

children.text: nāyakayugalakāvabhāse hi pratyuta lajjā jugupsāspṛhādisvocitacittavṛttyantarodayavyagratayākāśarasatvam athāpi syāt ||
children.translated_text: For when the pair of hero and heroine appears, on the contrary there might even be a tastelessness through distraction caused by the arising of other mental states proper to oneself, such as shame, disgust, longing, and so on.
Therefore cognition of rasa in the form of experience, memory, and the like is not reasonable.
The same objection applies also if it is produced.
If what previously existed in the form of a potency is later manifested, there follows gradation according to the acquisition of objects.
And whether it belongs to oneself, belongs to another, and so on must be considered as before.

children.text: tasmātkāvye doṣābhāvaguṇālaṃkāramayatvalakṣaṇena nāṭye caturvidhābhinayarūpeṇa nibiḍanijamohasaṃkaṭakāriṇā vibhāvādisādhāraṇīkaraṇātmanābhidhāto dvitīyenāṃśena bhāvakatvavyāpāreṇa bhāvyamāno raso 'nubhavasmṛtyādivilakṣaṇena rajastamo'nuvedhavaicitryabalād drutivistāravikāsalakṣaṇena sattvodrekaprakāśānandamayanijasaṃvidviśrāntilakṣaṇena parabrahmāsvādasavidhena bhogena paraṃ bhujyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, in poetry, through the absence of faults and through the constitution made of qualities and ornaments, and in drama, through the fourfold acting, which creates an intense constriction of one's own delusion, rasa is made an object of realization by the second part of denotation, namely the operation of making-real, whose nature is the universalization of determinants and so on; and it is supremely enjoyed by an enjoyment distinct from experience, memory, and the like, close to the savoring of the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, characterized by repose in one's own consciousness, which is full of the bliss of illumination from an upsurge of sattva and is marked by melting, expansion, and blossoming through the force of the varied penetration of rajas and tamas.

children.text: tatra pūrvapakṣo'yaṃ bhaṭṭalollaṭapakṣānabhyupagamād eva nābhyupagata iti taddūṣaṇam anutthānopahatam eva ||
children.translated_text: In this regard, this prima facie view has not been accepted simply because the position of <s>Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa</s> is not accepted; therefore the refutation of it is itself undermined by lack of occasion.

children.text: pratītyādivyatiriktaśca saṃsāre ko bhoga iti na vidmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And we do not know what enjoyment there is in worldly life apart from cognition and the like.
If one says, 'relishing,'
that too is simply a cognition.
Only, because of the distinctness of the means, let it be assigned a different name, just as there are different names such as seeing, inference, hearing, comparison, and intuition.

children.text: niṣpādanābhivyaktidvayānabhyupagame ca nityo vā asadvā rasa iti na tṛtīyā gatir asyām ||
children.translated_text: And if both production and manifestation are not accepted, then rasa is either eternal or nonexistent; there is no third course here.
And no unperceived thing exists that is fit for practical dealings.
Now it is said: cognition, as such, is the making of it into an object of enjoyment.
And that has the nature of prosperity and the like.
Let that be so.
Even so, it is not merely so much as that.

children.text: yāvanto hi rasāstāvanta eva rasanātmānaḥ pratītayo bhogīkaraṇasvabhāvāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For as many as the rasas are, just so many are the cognitions whose nature is savoring, having the character of being made into enjoyment.
And because the variety of principal and subsidiary relations among the qualities must be imagined as endless, there is a limitation only with regard to agency.

children.text: abhidhā bhāvanā cānyā tadbhogīkṛtam eva ca
children.translated_text: Denotation, imagination, and something else: that which has been made into enjoyment by it,
and when word, meaning, and ornamentation have reached the state of being the abode of denotation, then
this group beginning with <s>śṛṅgāra</s>, though itself to be brought into being by imagination, out of fear
pervades the successful person in the form made into enjoyment by that.
Thus.

children.text: yat kāvyena bhāvyante rasāḥ ityucyate tatra vibhāvādijanitacarvaṇātmakāsvādarūpapratyayagocaratāpādanam eva yadi bhāvanaṃ tadabhyupagamyata eva ||
children.translated_text: When it is said there, 'The rasas are brought into being by poetry,' if 'bringing into being' means only making them the object of a cognition in the form of relishful tasting produced by determinants and the rest, then that is indeed accepted.
But what was said is this:
'Rasa is the object of the supreme awareness, suggested and called cognition;
it is the experience whose nature is tasting, and is called the meaning of poetry.'
Thus.
There, by being suggested, it is characterized as the suggested meaning.
And through experience it should be understood as the object of that experience.
But if so, how can the reality of rasa stand?

children.text: adhunā raudrarasaṃ lakṣayati atha raudro nāmeti ||
children.translated_text: Now he defines the raudra rasa with the words, 'Now raudra by name.'
This is the intention behind the word 'self' here.
The doing of injustice is chiefly the object of anger.

children.text: tādṛśi ca jane sarvo 'pi manorathairapi rudhirapānamapi nāmādriyante ||
children.translated_text: And toward such a person everyone, even in his mere wishes, would even welcome drinking his blood.

children.text: tathā cāha lokaḥ tādṛśo yadi labhyate tattadīyaṃ rudhiramapi pītvā na tṛpyate ||
children.translated_text: Accordingly people say: if such a one is obtained, one is not satisfied even after drinking his blood.
The great poet <s>Bhāsa</s> too has said in his own composition:

children.text: tretāyugaṃ taddhi na maithilī sā rāmasya rāgapadavī mṛdu cāsya cetaḥ
children.translated_text: 'That indeed was the <s>Tretāyuga</s>; she was not <s>Maithilī</s>; <s>Rāma</s>'s path of passion, and his mind, were gentle.

children.text: labdhā janastu yadi rāvaṇasya kāyaṃ protkṛtya tanna tilaśo na vitṛptigāmī ||
children.translated_text: But if a man found the body of <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, even after tearing it out piece by piece he would not come to satisfaction.'
Thus.

children.text: tena hāsyavat sādhāraṇavibhāvatvāccarvaṇāpi krodhamayyeveti tadrasanācaraṇau raudraḥ krodhātmaka eva ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, since it has determinants common to all, as laughter does, the tasting too is entirely made of anger; hence the tasting and enactment of it are raudra, whose essence is anger itself.
Those in whom the propensity to kill is heightened are called violent or arrogant.
The actors who wear their costume are those persons.
Their nature is the cause for the arising of the savoring of this rasa.

children.text: atra vyācakṣate yuddhahetuka uddhatamanuṣyeṣu bhīmasenādiṣu rudhirapānādilakṣaṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here some explain: among violent men such as <s>Bhīmasena</s>, caused by battle, it is characterized by drinking blood and the like.
But rākṣasas and dānavas, they say, are naturally raudra.
That is wrong.
<s>Bhīma</s>'s drinking of blood is not caused by battle.
Rather, it is the reverse.

children.text: uddhatasvabhāvatvādeva hyasau krodhaparavaśaḥ sann anucitamapi pratijñātavān ||
children.translated_text: For because his nature is violent, he, being overpowered by anger, made even an improper vow.

children.text: tannirvāhāyaiva ca rākṣasādhiṣṭhānamasya kavinā veṇīsaṃhāre varṇitam ||
children.translated_text: And it is precisely for the fulfilment of that vow that the poet in the <s>Veṇīsaṃhāra</s> described his possession by a rākṣasa.
Therefore all these are angry by nature.

children.text: tadanusāriṇi naṭe raudra āsvādyata iti manuṣyaprakṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: When the actor conforms to that, raudra is tasted; thus its human type is established.

children.text: saṅgrāmahetuka iti cāyamarthaḥ yuddhasya kavinaṭapradarśyamānasya hetukaḥ kustitahetudhīrohitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the phrase 'caused by battle' has this meaning: the battle displayed by the poet and actor is its cause, while awareness of an improper cause is excluded.
The proper cause of it is not anger.

children.text: tathā ca prādhānyena yuddhena vīra eva vyapadekṣyate ||
children.translated_text: And so, when battle is predominant, it will rather be designated as vīra rasa.

children.text: nanvete svabhāvakrodhanā api kim uddīpanam apekṣante ||
children.translated_text: But do these, though angry by nature, still require stimulants?
He says yes, with the words 'and that.'
Anger and the rest are caused by another person.
Provocation means the dishonoring of wife and the like.
Insult is abuse of one's country, caste, lineage, learning, or occupation.
Falsehood is the utterance of some untrue statement.
Injury is the crushing down of house, servants, and so on.
Harshness of speech is threatening by mentioning killing and the like.
Hostility is the desire to kill.
Jealousy is resentment toward virtues.
By the word 'and so on' are included such things as seizure of a kingdom.
Through these, when they are described by the poet as determinants, it arises.

children.text: asya tāḍanādīni karmāṇi raktanayanādayo'nubhāvā iti pṛthaṅnirūpaṇaṃ tulye 'pyanubhāvatve viśeṣakhyāpanārtham ||
children.translated_text: For this rasa, actions such as striking are the activities, and red eyes and the like are the consequents; their separate exposition, although they are alike as consequents, is for the sake of indicating a distinction.
The distinction is that the former are to be described by words alone.
For they are not to be shown directly on the stage.
As will be said:
'Battle, loss of kingdom, death, and the besieging of a city
are to be arranged as things not done directly, by means of introductory scenes.'
Thus.
Red eyes and the like, however, are enacted directly on the stage.
But some say that the taking up of weapons was mistakenly read in the earlier passage.
Yet the purpose of stating this separately is slight.

children.text: ayaṃ cātrāśayaḥ rakṣodānavoddhatamanuṣyā uddīpanahetubhir vināpi ceṣṭitamātraṃ yadapi kurvate narmagoṣṭhyādyapi ca tatra tāḍanādi pradhānam ||
children.translated_text: The intention here is this: rākṣasas, dānavas, and violent humans, even without stimulating causes, whenever they do any mere act, even joking conversation and the like, striking and the rest are predominant there.
He will say this with the words, 'and whatever they undertake.'
When a stimulant is present, red eyes and the like become intensified, already seized by striking and the rest.
For this very reason the word 'again' is used.
There, striking is a blow with the palm and the like.
Splitting is making into two parts.
Pressing is crushing.
Cutting is severing.
Breaking is separating things from one another and the like.
The two words ending in -ṇyat are used in the sense of an action or state.
Taking up weapons means grasping them all around, on every side.
Now begins the section on bhayānaka rasa.
Because the heroic has fear as a subordinate component, he defines bhayānaka with the word 'now.'
A distorted cry is a loud laugh and the like.
The seeing of beings and <s>piśācas</s>.
Terror and agitation are directed toward another object.
Going to, that is, reaching, an empty house or a forest.
The seeing, by direct perception, of the killing and binding of one's own people.
Hearing is through tradition or report.
Stories and the like, even of things long past, are remembered through renewed recollection.

children.text: vepituṃ pravṛttaṃ yatkaracaraṇaṃ ādikarmaiva bhayavyañjakaṃ vyādhyādivailakṣaṇyasūcanāt ||
children.translated_text: The hands and feet that have begun to tremble are the very first action expressive of fear, since they indicate a difference from illness and the like.
<s>Pulaka</s> is the rising of the hair-pores, horripilation.
A break in the voice is an alteration of its natural condition.
The phrase is 'of the guru and the king.'
The intention is this: fear, first of all, will be stated to belong to women, low persons, children, and the like.
It does not belong to characters of the highest and middle type.

children.text: te'pi tu gurubhyo rājñaśca bhayaṃ darśayeyuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Yet they too may display fear toward gurus and toward the king.
Even in the absence of that, their excellence is all the more present in this way.
And ministers have no sovereignty.
As he says, 'acting as I please, I am indeed afraid.'

children.text: anubhāvāśca tathā śliṣṭāstatra kiyante loke yena satyata eva bhīto'yamiti gurvādīnāṃ pratītir bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And in that case the consequents are so closely fitted, and to such a degree, in ordinary life, that gurus and the others form the cognition, 'This man is truly afraid.'
And because it is unnatural, it has artificiality; and because, when continued for too long, it is not relishable, it has the status of <s>rasa</s> only in that way.
Nor does it have the status of a transitory state.

children.text: taddhi tadā syādyadi svabhāvata eva na kiṃcitkālalavam utpādyate ||
children.translated_text: For that would be so only if, by nature, it were not produced even for a tiny fraction of time.
The alteration of the limbs and so on is a reversal of color, activity, posture, and the like.
The phrase 'looking, he passes by' means that the act of looking is made with eyes unmarked, as if by one terrified and eager to flee.
<s>Udvega</s> is trembling or movement.
<s>Sāda</s> is the slackness of the limbs.
There is dryness of the mouth at the palate.
There is pounding of the heart with excessive speed.

children.text: iha bhayam ityabhineyamiti vīrarasa ityāryātaḥ sambadhyate ||
children.translated_text: Here the statement 'fear is to be acted' is connected from the verse on the heroic <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: tā etā hyāryā ekapraghaṭṭakatayā pūrvācāryair lakṣaṇatvena paṭhitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For these verses were recited by earlier teachers as definitions in a single connected section.
But the sage placed them in their proper places for easy collection.
The phrase is 'arisen from <s>sattva</s>'.
<s>Sattva</s> is concentration of the mind; what is born from that is meant. This is an instruction for the actor.
And the commentator says that it applies to every object.
This is incorrect.
This whole chapter is solely for the instruction of poets and actors.
For in ordinary life there is no practical usage of determinants, consequents, acting, and the like.

children.text: tasmād ayamatrārthaḥ etat tāvad bhayasvabhāvajaṃ rajastamaḥprakṛtīnāṃ nīcānāmityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the meaning here is this: this, to begin with, is born from the nature of fear and belongs to low persons whose constitution is made of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>.

children.text: ye'pi ca sattvapradhānāsteṣāṃ sattvasamutthaṃ prayatnakṛtamebhirevānubhāvaiḥ kāryam ||
children.translated_text: But even those in whom <s>sattva</s> predominates should produce what is arisen from <s>sattva</s>, deliberately, through these very consequents.
However, they should do so with gentle gestures, since that is artificial.
The word 'again' indicates a distinction.

children.text: nanu ca rājādi kimiti gurvādibhyo bhayaṃ kṛtakaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object, why does a king and the like display artificial fear before gurus and the like?
And after displaying it, why does he show gentle trembling of the limbs and so forth?
And why is artificiality mentioned precisely in the case of the fearful?
For the artificiality of everything has been stated.

children.text: yathā veśyā dhanārthinīti kṛtakāṃ ratim ādarśayati ityāśaṅkya sādhāraṇamuttaram āha tathaiva kāryamiti ||
children.translated_text: For example, a courtesan, desiring money, shows artificial love. Anticipating this objection, he gives a general answer: 'it should be done in just that way.'
For when fear has been displayed, the guru recognizes him as disciplined.
And, because of the gentleness of the gestures, he counts him as a person of inferior nature.
From artificial erotic love taught by courtesans there is no achievement of any human aim.
For only by the very method that has been stated is a specific practical human aim obtained.

children.text: yatra tu rājā na kṛtakaṃ parānugrahāya krodhavismayādīndarśayati tatra vyabhicāritaiva teṣāṃ na sthāyitetyetadarthaḥ sūcikāmeva guruvaṃśāntaraprasiddhām āryāṃ paṭhati karacaraṇeti ||
children.translated_text: But where the king does not artificially display anger, wonder, and the like for the sake of favoring others, there those states have only the status of transitory states, not of stable states. To indicate this meaning, he recites the verse 'hands and feet,' well known in another lineage of teachers, merely as an indicator.
The word is 'always'.
Both when it is artificial and when it is not artificial.
Thus ends the section on the <s>bhayānaka-rasa</s>.
